elite (read as old school usenet) decide there is a problem with the
official rules. It is met with thoughtful respect from the powers that
be and initiates a constructive discussion.(note the recent rules
argument between James Coupe and LSJ) However when anyone else belives

force the opposing positon to simply give up as they have met the
large immovable object that is the VTES elite general concensus. this
has happened to me on more than one occasion which is why I generally
lurk rather than post anymore.

As far as the CL/NCL debate is concerned I agree with some arguments
on both sides *Quiet pause as many feign shock* the game was designed
with nolimits and as I see it this as neccasary for the following
reason...

In magic you can limit the cards because you only have to defeat a
single opponent in tournament play so with four of each card getting
your winning combo off is a likely occurance and somewhat balanced.
With VTES however you have up to six other players to be concerned
with and with only four copys of your great ousting combo in the deck
you can only see it acctually come up in a usefull order four times.
realisticly you will only get it twice if that and 2 VP's cannot
garantee you a victory. so four of a given card is not enough thus the
basic no limit argument as I see it from a tournament perspective.

now on the other hand the basic argument of the CL camp is ridiculous
repitition I can see the point here because from a tournament
perspective some heavily repetitive decks require zero skill to win
with I want to win or lose a tournament based on the playing skill of
my opponents not the "cheesyness" of there deck. I have a deck in the
yahoo archive ( deck name "Little Ones" if you care) that is a very
good deck however it requires zero skill to play and win with I can
take any player with a simplistic understanding of the game give them
this deck and enter them in a tourny and they will honestly have a
decent shot at doing quite well. This is very bad for the game IMHO
because they are not a good enough player to be a tournament winner.
the fact that the world champ could one day be a 12 year old who
happend to pick the right flavor of cheese cannot be good for the game
as a whole.

I honestly belive the reason this argument keeps coming up is not
because either side is wrong or right but because the game needs some
sort of compromise between both camps to acchive the ever sought after
balance I don't honestly belive that will ever happen simply due to
the large immovable object I spoke of earlier.

ok I'll shut up now and go back to lurking

Eric

I've brought this up before, and maybe it's time to bring this up again.
We have a FAQ. It's almost time that maybe we should have a FOCS:
Frequently Offered Clever Suggestions. On it we can put Concealed
Weapon, card limits, etc., in nauseating detail, with the arguments for
and against. And in the FAQ we can say "Refer to the FOCS for the
details regarding your idea, and if you haven't anything new to say that
isn't discussed in there, please put a lid on it", ... except we can
probably say it much more politely.

See, the problem is, that general consensus was arrived at by several
YEARS of back-and-forth about these very arguments. Concealed Weapon
has been hashed out and beaten into the ground on many different
occasions. So have card limits, but even MORE so. Everyone gets
frosted because we're very, VERY tired of repeating what, to us, is
already demonstrated fact... because I can assure you I haven't heard
ANYTHING new out of the "fix CW" or "make a CL" camps this time around
that hasn't already been said and countered at some point in the past.
And it's not good that we tend to respond with a bit more vitriol than
we should, but REALLY, people always want to stand up and believe that
somehow, we haven't thought of something or that nobody's made the
argument before, when yes, it HAS been said.

a FOCS would certainly be much easier than saying "go look in Google",
as nobody bothers to look in Google to find the old debates... which is
irritating to us, since we really don't want to have to go forth and
write all of it out AGAIN, over and over.

--
Derek

There's the point we find difficult to get across to xCL players, and
are largely forced to rely on testimony from ex-xCL players (say it
fast) to handle. Any deck that turns itself into too much of a
one-trick pony (20 Majesties) will find itself in severe trouble when
its trick gets derailed; what happens when the deck sits in front of a
deck that takes a whole lot of Corruption and other stealth actions, and
sits behind a deck that is full of voter-bloat and Deflection? It won't
ever get into combat, and it'll die miserably with a handful of Majesty.

Most people usually figure out very quickly that playing decks like this
turns too much over to the realm of chance (sit next to an IG deck, and
die), and moderate their building style after awhile to be more robust
and immune to the vagaries of seating position. I know I generally
build decks very heavy-handedly at first (large globs of the Primary
Trick), and trim out as appropriate after the first couple times I play
it, while adding in whatever support cards I've found to be lacking.
Very rarely do I leave a deck with more than 10 of any given card in it,
and very rarely do I ever even BUILD a deck with 10 of any *two* given
cards. It just isn't effective -- and it's quite amusing that Andrew's
analysis shows that the self-limitation of NCL players generally ends up
around 10 as well, barring special cases (Corruption, Cryptic Mission,
etc).

I have experience of several CCG and think that it's easier to build a
"robot" deck for this game than others. The reasons for this are:

1. Your deck can be totally prey-focussed - it can ignore all the other
players and still be effective. Without the bleed-left rule, you tend
to get more player-interaction in other multi-player games.

2. NCL means that you can have high multiples of few cards so that
little to no choice is required when deciding what to play. E.g. the
Computer Hacking/Effective Management weenie deck. This also eliminates
the problem of shuffling - the deck has little randomness.
Paradoxically, this lack of luck decreases the amount of skill required
to play.

3. It's not strictly necessary to win - doing well may be enough in
many events. You only need to score one VP for an average performance.

Peter Bajika published a winning deck at the weekend that seemed quite
formulaic. The library was mostly made up of six cards which I think I
can recall from memory - they are such clichés. They were: Minion Tap,
5th Tradition, Majesty, Obedience, Telepathic Misdirection and Kine
Resources Contested. In addition, it had seven Anarch Revolt and a
crypt full of high-cap vampires. I'm no expert but I think I got the
hang of that deck without any explanation. An algorithm for playing it
wouldn't be very lengthy.

have houserules in casual play, and there is nothing to say against

of nominating a Prince (*if there is not already one in the city*).

to the VEKN, though we *encourage* play by the official rules, so
players have it easier to partake in tournaments and can use their
decks in other domains as well. VTES is an *extremely* international
CCG, which can be seen by the large number of tournament-tourists. :)

The VEKN has a total of 2546 players in 176 domains all around the
world. Of these domains, 82% play without any houserules (in private
games), and 11% play with a CL of any sort (in private games). (The
missing 6% gave no indication whether they use CL or not.)
Percentage wise, the largest CL-using areas are South America and the
Pacific Region (see Prince-listing on WW HP).
Also, large groups tend to be using NL (in private games), while small
groups are more inclined to a CL of any sort (in private games).
Europe has 16% CL users, North America has 6%, whereas the two largest
domains in the world (Barcelona, Spain, and L.A., US use no
house-rules).

Because the ability to construct crypts is half the ability to construct
playing decks. If a library card is unobtainable, there's some number of decks
you can't build. If it's a relatively specialized one, the decks are small in
number and very narrowly focused. I believe that the lack of any given vampire,
let alone a number of them, is going to tend to affect someone's ability to
construct a lot more types of decks (or construct them effectively). The
inaccessibility of a lot of Tremere Antitribu vampires to newer players is
likely affecting more players' attempts to build Thaumaturgy and possibly certain
types of Auspex decks much more so than being unable to obtain things like
Shotgun Rituals.

This obviously isn't a hard and fast rule. Rarify the more common cards that
could be considered staple cards and their lack will probably have a stronger
effect on things than any single vampire. Freak Drive could possibly be
considered a staple card that should be more common. Thus I would guess that
it's rarity is having a fairly significant effect on a lot of players. By the
same token, I suppose in some ways those 11-cap vampires being on the high end
of the age spectrum probably makes them more specialized than most crypt cards
and thus better candidates for things a collection can do without than, say, a
six cap with strong in-clan disciplines. But in general, I believe vampire
variety is more important to players than the vast majority of relatively
specialized rare library cards.

>

> same rarity, AIUI.

criticizing the rarity levels of these vampires in The Sabbat. It's just that
the way things have gone with those particular vampire cards has had an
unfortunate effect, IMO.

> > That's bad.
>
> I don't see collectability as inherently bad.
> The demand for certain library cards is higher than that for others, as well.
> So long as the cards are balanced, this isn't a bad thing.

Collectability is not inherently bad. (Well, if I had my druthers, customizable
card games would not be collectible. Unfortunately, I suspect that's not a
realistic hope given the economic practicalities. Anyway, it's a different
subject altogether.) But you have to call your shots about which cards are easy
to obtain and which are the ones that people have to hunt and peck for. If you
make it too hard to build _any_ kind of viable, competitive deck without being a
Mr. Suitcase then you'll discourage the players with more modest investments
from playing at all. I'm afraid if you were to follow Mr. Davidson's suggestion,
that might well become a problem.

Fred
